He held him steady until the spasms passed. “You’re one lucky bastard, you know that?” Jake coughed so hard he nearly vomited. He sagged into Orela’s hold as he caught his breath. “She moved the fucking floor.” His voice had a quality to it that hadn't been there before — stripped of the arrogant edge it had earlier, raw underneath. "I felt it shift. I knew She was in the building and I stepped on it anyway and She just—" He stopped. "It was just playing with me. It had me and it was just—" "It’s ok. You're out," Orela ran her hand over his leg, assessing the cut with quick professional focus. “It’s not deep, Messy, but not deep. You’ll be fine, so long as whatever’s in this water doesn’t give you a random infection.” Jake looked at the hole. At the water lapping at its edge with that same patient quality it had had all night. “I’ve had worse,” Jake muttered, wiping his face and wincing as Orela tied his bandana around the cut, slowing the bleed to a more reasonable level. Dwight stared at them both, still breathing too fast as anxiety clamped around him. David kept a hand on Leon’s shoulder, not to steady him anymore — but to ground himself. The hallway fell into a quiet tension. Just the sound of their breath. The creak of the building. And the water lapping, steady as ever, just behind them. From the classroom doorway, Danny’s phone caught everything; the thrash of the beam below water, the long, terrifying silence, the sudden eruption of two soaked survivors clawing back to life. He zoomed in, framed it perfectly. On the RC feed from his submersible, the lens had tracked them the whole way, Jake’s bubbles scattering, Leon’s frantic dive, the scramble back to air. A perfect double angle. Danny chuckled low into his mask, whispering like a delighted commentator. "And there it is, back from the brink. Lucky boys. She’s playing with you now! Better get a move on." He zoomed in. Framed it. Waited. Ch 7 – Floodgate The back door was worse than the front. That shouldn't have been possible. The front door had been a wall wearing a door's memory — swollen past function, the frame warped into something that had forgotten what gaps were for. But this one had gone further, past bloated and into something that looked almost geological. The wood had darkened to near-black, grain split in long weeping lines, the surface slick and soft in places where it had absorbed so much water it had stopped being wood in any meaningful sense. The metal was gone entirely — hinges, handle, strike plate, all of it reduced to rust-colored suggestions fused permanently to the frame. Even the seam where door met wall had disappeared, the entire frame curled outward like it had been soaking for decades. David hit it anyway. Shoulder first, weight behind it, the impact landing with that same swallowed quality that everything in this building produced — force going in, nothing coming back. Leon followed with a length of shelving, the metal edge finding no purchase on a surface too soft to catch and too solid to dent. Jake worked the bottom with his boot, then his knee, then his boot again. The water climbed past their hips and shifted with every impact, sloshing back against their legs like a rebuttal. The crowbar was gone. Somewhere in the hallway, or the particular pocket of dark water that had taken Jake and had likely kept what fell out of his hands as a consolation prize. They were down to bodies and debris, and the door received both with the same patient indifference. Dwight had his back to the wall, arms wrapped tight against himself. His eyes kept flicking down to the water creeping up his legs, the anxiety sucking at his ribs. The flow had quieted — not stagnant, but sluggish — dragged thin across the endless sprawl of the building. It left behind a slick murk clinging to corners, swallowing dropped tools and broken tile alike. It crawled up the grout — slow but certain. He watched it tick past a screw left embedded in the tile. Then past a crack in the plaster. His lips moved again, quieter, a whisper under his breath. "Five... there’s five of us. There shouldn’t be five." The others didn’t notice, too caught in the rhythm of smashing and straining. Their grunts filled the hallway. The sharp clang of a metal desk leg on rotted wood. The curse of another wasted swing. But Dwight’s eyes were wide, haunted, thoughts spiraling. “Four survivors,” he whispered. “Two gates. Four skills. Two exits. Always balance. Always ritual. The Entity loved symmetry. So why...” He trailed off. Five people. His lips moved silently, mumbling, counting. Five. It’s never five. Why? The question chased its own tail. He pressed his palm flat against the wall behind him, feeling the damp of it, and tried to find the shape of what was nagging at him. The math was ruthless but it was clean. It accounted for everyone. Five didn't account for everyone. His eyes moved across the group without meaning to, cataloguing. David. Leon. Jake. Orela. Is one of us not meant to— He didn't finish the thought. Pressed it back down, hard, and fixed his gaze on the door like that would help. Down the hall, Danny had found himself a perch.
